title: Clients that depend on one role each

blocks.text: A client that only submits tasks should not see `shutdown()` or the monitoring methods; a component that manages the lifecycle should not see `submit()`. The page segregates a concurrent executor into **roles**, and one class implements them all:
In `Roles` the three role interfaces are given. Write:

items: `ManagedExecutor(poolSize)`, on a fixed thread pool: `submit` runs a task on one of the pool's threads, never on the caller's, and counts it in `getCompletedCount()` only once it has finished (a task that throws has finished too), not when it is submitted; `shutdown()` shuts the pool down, so its threads end; `isShutdown()` says whether it was shut down. As the page's edge case says, a task submitted **after shutdown is refused** with `IllegalStateException`, guarded by an `AtomicBoolean`;
`TaskClient`, which only submits: `runTask(task)` submits it and returns its future;
`LifecycleManager`, which only manages the lifecycle: `gracefulShutdown()` and `isRunning()`.

blocks.text: The starter's two clients take a whole `ManagedExecutor`. **Each client's one constructor must take only the role interface it uses**, so it can be handed anything that plays that role.

cases.says: A client runs two tasks, both are counted, and a manager shuts the executor down.
TaskClient's constructor takes a TaskSubmitter and LifecycleManager's takes a LifecycleManageable.
A task submitted after shutdown is refused with IllegalStateException.
A task that throws has finished too: it is counted once its failure is in.

concepts: In a concurrent executor, a client that submits tasks depends only on a submitter role and a lifecycle manager only on a lifecycle role, while one class implements all the roles.
The managed executor refuses a task submitted after shutdown, guarded by an AtomicBoolean.
